I look out my window right now and see the moon. While the moon wasn't built by women, of course, it was the staging area for what is widely regarded in the international scientific community as the single most significant achievement of the Human race to date: the Apollo Program.

Margaret Hamilton, the individual regarded as having coined the term "software engineering," was a self taught computer programmer who ran the Software engineering department at MIT. She curated all and single-handedly wrote much of the programming code for the Apollo Guidance Computer, which ran on one of the first ever chip-based computers. The stakes being so incredibly high, and the code being largely written by hand, the margin of error was impossibly small. The success of the Apollo missions would have never been realized without the genius and diligence of this woman and her profound ability. She is pictured here with the printouts of the code developed by her team for the famous Apollo 11 mission.

While I'm already staring at the moon, almost all of Miss Hamilton's code for the Apollo Guidance Computer had to be based on and populated with impossibly precise and complex mathematical calculation developed by the sharpest mathematicians in the world, many of whom were women working long hours in small teams.

There were more than a few women who also passed all requirements and obligations as test pilots to qualify as astronauts, though in the 50's and 60's women were procedurally excluded from consideration for the position.
